hints: Focus on the word always, so look for the one definition of oxidation that works in every single case, not just some cases.
Remember OILRIG for electrons: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain, so the species being oxidised must lose electrons.
Think about what losing negative electrons does to the charge or oxidation number of an atom, and pick the statement that matches that change.
walkthrough:
**Recall the three ways to define oxidation**

Oxidation can be described as gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, or loss of electrons. The most general and always true definition uses electrons and oxidation numbers.

Remember OILRIG: $$\text{Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons}$$

**Check why oxygen and electron gain fail**

Gain of oxygen is only true for some oxidations. Many oxidations involve no oxygen at all, for example $\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+} + e^-$.

Similarly, the species oxidised loses electrons, it does not gain them. Gaining electrons is reduction.

**Link electron loss to oxidation number**

When an atom loses negative electrons, it becomes more positive. So its oxidation number must go up.

That is: $$\text{oxidation = loss of } e^- = \text{increase in oxidation number}$$ This is true in every oxidation reaction.

options.A: Gain of oxygen is one example of oxidation, but not always true. Many oxidations involve only electron loss with no oxygen, such as $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$.
options.B: Usually oxidation and reduction happen together, but they do not need a different reactant. In disproportionation the same reactant is both oxidised and reduced, for example chlorine in the reaction with cold $\text{NaOH}$.
options.C: This is backwards and describes reduction. By OILRIG, the species being oxidised loses electrons, while the species being reduced gains electrons.
options.D: This is the universal definition. Oxidation is loss of electrons, and losing negative charge makes the oxidation number more positive, so it always increases.
